results.title: Your Thunderbolt port can be used to steal data from a locked PC — here's the setting that stops it
results.author: Afam Onyimadu
results.content:
When you turn on your computer and reach the Windows lock screen, it feels like a solid barrier. It isn't. You're prompted to enter a password before access is granted. However, Thunderbolt or USB4 devices may still potentially access system memory on some Windows PCs. Many devices have a built-in mechanism that defends against this kind of intrusion, and you can check whether it's working for you in a single System Information field.
The lock screen doesn't stop every kind of hardware access
A locked screen doesn't erase sensitive data from RAM
When Windows is locked, it limits what a user can do via the keyboard, mouse, and desktop. But a connected PCIe device isn't automatically limited in what it can do with the system's memory.
This is a significant difference, since pressing Win + L doesn't automatically empty the system RAM. Processes running before the lock may still have sensitive information in memory, including authentication materials or other data an attacker could target. That information doesn't disappear simply because it's hidden behind a lock screen.
This leads us to Thunderbolt and USB4. They can expose PCIe-connected peripherals capable of Direct Memory Access (DMA), allowing them to read or write system memory without CPU intervention.
The point isn't that plugging in a random Thunderbolt accessory means an intruder immediately walks away with all the information in RAM. The extent of effectiveness usually depends on the accessory's driver and Windows' DMA protection.
A password prompt controls who can use the OS, but it doesn't control how far an external device can reach.
Kernel DMA Protection restricts what external devices can access
Kernel DMA Protection uses the IOMMU to restrict DMA
Kernel DMA Protection is a hardware- and firmware-dependent security feature. Modern chipsets come with an Input-Output Memory Management Unit (IOMMU), a gatekeeper between expansion devices and physical system memory (RAM). Windows ensures the IOMMU assigns DMA-capable peripherals to specific memory regions, preventing unrestricted access to RAM.
Once Kernel DMA Protection is enabled, devices with DMA remapping drivers can still perform DMA while the screen is locked, but the IOMMU restricts them to the memory regions assigned to them. However, devices without DMA remapping support cannot initiate DMA while the screen is locked.
Older interfaces like FireWire, PCMCIA, CardBus, or ExpressCard are not covered by Kernel DMA Protection.
Rather than assuming Windows automatically blocks every Thunderbolt device while the screen is locked, the protection distinguishes between peripherals whose drivers support DMA remapping and those that don't.
Kernel DMA Protection only takes effect after Windows loads; before that, the system firmware provides protection, so pre-boot vulnerabilities may still exist.
Kernel DMA Protection depends on the PC's UEFI and hardware support, so two laptops that look almost identical may have different security capabilities.
System Information knows if yours is protected
Check Kernel DMA Protection in System Information
There is a simple way to verify whether your computer has Kernel DMA Protection. Follow these steps:
- Press Win + R, type MSInfo32, and press Enter.
- Look through the System Summary for Kernel DMA Protection.
"On" implies that the platform supports the feature, and it's already enabled on the device. Supported systems usually enable Kernel DMA Protection automatically, so there isn't a separate switch to turn it on.
If it shows 'Off,' that doesn't mean you disabled a Windows setting — Kernel DMA Protection depends on the platform, firmware, and IOMMU support. On some systems, enabling the required virtualization and I/O virtualization options in UEFI can resolve this; on others, the hardware simply doesn't support the feature.
The results you see on MSInfo32 give you exactly what the PC reports as opposed to what the manufacturer advertised before you bought it.
Kernel DMA Protection isn't the only DMA defense
Once Kernel DMA Protection is enabled, don't try to hunt for other ways to make the feature protect your device better.
If Kernel DMA Protection is "Off," you can choose alternatives depending on your hardware and firmware. On certain systems, there are Thunderbolt security controls in UEFI. For systems that don't use Kernel DMA Protection, Microsoft also documents older BitLocker DMA countermeasures. Alternatives are platform-specific and are not universal fixes; apply them only when they're appropriate for your hardware and firmware.
Drive-by DMA attacks may only take a few minutes and may not even require opening the computer. However, Kernel DMA Protection isn't a general defense against firmware attacks, pre-boot attacks, or malware that is already running on the system. Also, if a bad actor has adequate physical access, they may still be able to tamper with the actual machine.
Aside from a laptop simply having a Thunderbolt port, the real question is whether the OS and port hardware can prevent external devices from gaining unrestricted access to memory.
results.summary:
Windows users should verify their Kernel DMA Protection status in System Information to ensure Thunderbolt and USB4 devices cannot bypass lock screen security to access system memory.

### Key Points
- Windows lock screens do not automatically prevent PCIe-connected peripherals from accessing system RAM via Direct Memory Access (DMA).
- Kernel DMA Protection uses an Input-Output Memory Management Unit (IOMMU) to restrict external devices to specific, safe memory regions.
- Users can check their security status by typing "MSInfo32" in the Windows Run dialog and locating the "Kernel DMA Protection" field.
- The feature is hardware-dependent and requires specific UEFI and chipset support, meaning it cannot be manually enabled on incompatible systems.
- Older interfaces like FireWire and ExpressCard are not covered by Kernel DMA Protection, leaving them vulnerable to unauthorized memory access.

### Why it Matters
This security feature is critical for protecting sensitive data, such as authentication credentials, from physical "drive-by" attacks using malicious peripherals. Understanding your device's DMA protection status helps identify potential hardware vulnerabilities that remain active even when a computer is locked.

results.title: 4 ways I secured my Plex server before exposing it to the internet
results.author: Jasmine Mannan
results.content:
A default Plex setup has you enabling remote access in your server settings and then automatically triggering Universal Plug and Play, which opens external port 32400 directly through your router's firewall.
Many users do this without realizing why default exposure is dangerous. Automated web bots and search engines continuously scan public IPv4 ranges for open 32400 end ports, probing for unpatched media server vulnerabilities, API exposure, and brute force targets.
Safely exposing a media server requires moving beyond default settings by routing traffic through a hard and reverse proxy, enforcing strict access controls and strong authentication, isolating Plex on its own network, and automating update cycles. You can stream your library anywhere without compromising your home network.
Reverse proxy
Don't use default port 32400
Pillar number one for ensuring the best security when using Plex is to route traffic through a reverse proxy. Default port 32400 has a major flaw. Raw port forwarding is an antipattern. Exposing default application ports directly tells any port scanner exactly which service is running on your IP address. Instead, you could use a reverse proxy shield like Caddy or Nginx.
A reverse proxy sits between WAN traffic and your media server. This means it restricts incoming traffic to standard HTTPS using a custom subdomain. It can also enforce modern TLS 1.3 encryption and automated Let's Encrypt certificate management, and it hides internal server IP addresses and port types from the public internet.
To activate this, you have to use custom server access URLs in Plex. Go to your Plex server's Settings, then hit Network, and then you should see custom server access URLs. Official mobile, desktop, and smart TV apps should automatically connect through your encrypted reverse proxy rather than raw IP handshakes.
Passwords should be secure
And make use of mandatory 2FA
Pillar number two is hardening authentication and limiting server access. Whenever you're using Plex, the best course of action is to ensure you use a strong password and enable mandatory 2FA for your root account. Enforce complex, unique master passwords backed by two-factor authentication to eliminate credential-stuffing vulnerabilities.
You can also tighten your Plex-specific access controls. For example, in your settings, you can enable secure connections so they are always required. By default, it appears as preferred, but changing it to required can block unencrypted plain-text HTTP fallbacks.
Another crucial step is to wipe the Networks Allowed Without Authentication settings. Ensure that the LAN IP Exception box in Plex Network settings is empty to prevent compromised local devices from accessing server controls without logging in. You can also use Plex Home and Managed Accounts properly so you never have to share primary admin credentials with household members or anyone else you grant access to. By creating separate profiles, you can grant library access scope and disable remote deletion rights for non-admin profiles, providing an extra layer of security.
VLAN segmentation can make a big difference
Keep the rest of your home secure
Another step you can take, known as Pillar 3, is to isolate Plex on your local network. If you're running an unpatched media server, it's compromised on a flat network. An attacker gains immediate local access to your NAS storage, primary workstation, and sensitive smart home devices, making it a complete hazard. By using VLAN segmentation, you can place the media server in an isolated DMZ or server VLAN so that if it ever gets remotely accessed by a hacker, they don't have access to the rest of your network, either.
Also, enforce strict firewall rules on your router to allow Plex to respond only to established/related sessions and block the Plex server from initiating outbound connections to your private home LAN.
In addition to isolating Plex on your local network, you can isolate the container. There are some best practices you can use for Docker permissions and read-only volume mounts to keep Plex safe. You can mount media storage libraries as read-only, so a compromised container cannot alter or encrypt your media files. You can run the container under a non-root user ID, helping keep your files safe.
Updates are crucial
One missed patch can introduce vulnerabilities
The last pillar for you to follow is to make sure you keep Plex and any other underlying infrastructure you use up to date. There's a major cost to patch delays. Media servers process untrusted external network inputs, audio/video codecs, and metadata passes, making zero-day patches critical. You're dealing with a lot of files that may not be 100% secure, so having the extra layer of protection is absolutely fundamental.
You can make use of automated container patching. Modern update pipelines, such as Watchtower or automated Docker Compose rollouts, can automatically pull official Plex image updates and restart the service with zero downtime. This way, you don't even have to intervene to ensure you have the latest patch installed.
Alongside this, keeping host Linux kernels, Intel Quick Sync drivers, and NVIDIA container toolkits up to date is just as important as updating the Plex application layer itself. All of these layers are vulnerable when they're not fully updated with the latest patches and security details.
Don't risk your security for self-hosted media
Protect your Plex server
Remote media streaming is one of the most rewarding self-hosted projects, but convenience shouldn't come at the expense of your home network perimeter. Ensure that when you are using Plex, you have security measures in place to protect yourself. You can do this by closing port 32400, putting Plex behind a reverse proxy, and isolating its container on a separate VLAN. And enjoy your personal media streaming setup with complete peace of mind.
results.summary:
Plex users are urged to move beyond default remote access settings by implementing reverse proxies and network segmentation to protect their home servers from automated web-based security threats.

### Key Points
- Disable default port 32400 forwarding to prevent automated bots from identifying and probing your media server for vulnerabilities.
- Deploy a reverse proxy like Caddy or Nginx to enforce HTTPS encryption and hide internal server details from the public internet.
- Enable mandatory two-factor authentication and set secure connections to "required" to block unencrypted HTTP fallbacks and credential-stuffing attacks.
- Use VLAN segmentation to isolate the media server in a DMZ, preventing attackers from accessing other sensitive devices on your local network.
- Implement automated patching tools like Watchtower to ensure the Plex application and underlying container infrastructure remain updated against zero-day exploits.

### Why it Matters
Relying on default configurations leaves home networks vulnerable to unauthorized access and potential data breaches through exposed media server ports. Implementing these security layers allows users to enjoy remote streaming while significantly reducing the risk of compromising their broader home infrastructure.

results.title: Consulting's race to become AI native
results.author: Polly Thompson
results.content:
It's a question as old as the industry itself: What does a consultant actually do?
Traditionally, consultants have acted as an external support system, called in to crunch the numbers, trim head count, or identify growth opportunities.
Now, AI is reshaping what clients want from consultants and how work gets done, creating a new job profile that blurs the lines between tech and consulting.
Instead of generalist teams producing research and strategy decks, consultants are increasingly expected to provide something tangible: tools, systems, and holistic, ongoing support. The big firms aren't only advising on tech strategy, they're building and implementing it, often through multi-year transformation projects.
To win that work, consulting firms are racing to position themselves as "AI-native."
"The more they're perceived to be a technology firm, the more likely they are to win business," Fiona Czerniawska, CEO of Source Global, a consulting sector intelligence firm, told Business Insider.
But the transformation raises a key question: Are these companies fundamentally changing what they do, or merely how they describe themselves?
The race to become AI-native
Looking back at the top firms' actions and rhetoric over the past year makes clear just how central AI has become to the consulting business.
"There is no doubt that our firm is a tech company that delivers now on audit, tax, and advisory services," Tim Walsh, CEO of KPMG US, told Business Insider's Dan DeFrancesco at the World Economic Forum in January.
For the fourth-largest professional services firm in the US, with roots reaching back to 1897, Walsh's statement was striking. A decade ago, KPMG would have described itself as a time-and-materials business with "smart people doing smart things," Rob Fisher, vice chairman of advisory at KPMG, said about Walsh's comments.
Now, the firm is embedding AI across its traditional offerings, while responding to growing client demand for subscription-style products, alongside advice and managed services, said Fisher. "We have to become more of a technology organization because clients want to consume our expertise that way," Fisher said.
KPMG isn't an outlier.
PwC has rewritten its training agenda around 30 core skills: 15 AI-centric and 15 human-centric, both of which are "extremely critical" to its success, Yolanda Seals-Coffield, chief people and inclusion officer for PwC US, told Business Insider in February.
EY is using AI as a training assistant to help its staff anticipate how their roles will evolve, and McKinsey has started using Lilli, its internal AI chatbot, in its recruitment process.
Allison Heithoff, a consultant with five years of experience, has seen the change firsthand.
Before AI, most of Heithoff's consulting job was "hands-to-keyboard work." In her first years at the midsize firm West Monroe, she spent her time gathering client data, configuring systems, developing features, testing them, and deploying them.
Five years later, AI can do a lot of that work.
The shift has made her role more strategy-focused and technical. Heithoff, who studied business administration, has found herself using AI to code and develop client solutions in ways she never expected.
Consultancies are hiring differently, too, looking to fill their ranks with deeply skilled technologists. Recent annual reports show that Accenture — already known for its technology capabilities — has added nearly 40,000 AI and data professionals in the last two years, and EY has added 61,000 technologists since 2023.
In February, PwC introduced a new career track for the first time in its 170-year history: the engineering track. The move is a "signpost" for where PwC expects future value to be created, Matt Wood, the firm's then-chief technology and innovation officer, told Business Insider. (Wood left the firm in May).
Even the language of consulting is changing. As Business Insider reported in January, Deloitte is outright scrapping titles like "analyst" and "consultant" and giving all US employees more specific job titles.
Tech and consulting are bleeding into each other
Underpinning all of this is a deeper shift in what consulting firms do and the tools they use to do it.
The largest consultancies have struck multibillion-dollar partnerships with the biggest names in AI, such as OpenAI, Nvidia, Anthropic, and Microsoft, to build internal tools that automate work once handled by junior staff. Now they are rolling out networks of AI agents for employees, and launching AI-enhanced platforms to give clients direct access to their expertise.
The work is also starting to look different. The strategy consulting firm BCG reported in April that AI- and tech-focused services now account for over 40% of its total global revenue, driven by a 25% year-on-year growth in AI services. At McKinsey, AI initiatives now account for roughly 40% of the firm's work, Alex Singla, a senior partner who co-leads QuantumBlack, McKinsey's AI arm, told Business Insider in January.
It's the kind of implementation work that tech companies often do with their own products. Last year, OpenAI launched its own consulting wing, offering clients tailored products and implementation support. Palantir, a tech company that sells software platforms, has teams of "forward-deployed engineers" and "customer success teams" that provide hands-on implementation and strategic advisory services to clients. (Palantir also partners with traditional consulting firms like Bain, PwC, and Accenture.)
Add in the surge of new AI-powered consulting startups — betting that AI can do strategy work just as easily as a team of consultants — and the lines between the two worlds get blurrier.
KPMG's Fisher said the firm's leadership team is out on the West Coast and Silicon Valley every six weeks to "stay connected to the action," meeting with founders, venture capital firms, and their large alliance partners. Previously, business development teams on the West Coast and client conversations would help senior leaders keep abreast of technology shifts.
The result of all this tech evolution is partnerships galore between the top firms and AI leaders. Consulting firms have become critical intermediaries in the AI boom, giving top AI companies access to a vast roster of Fortune 500 clients who still want to turn to a traditional firm for breadth of services, sector expertise, and global reach.
From the early internet to cybersecurity to SaaS, consulting has adapted to technology before, layering fresh capabilities onto a familiar model. The difference now, industry insiders say, is that technology capabilities are becoming table stakes for all firms and evolving faster than ever.
Over the past decade, technology integration evolved gradually, Tony Farnfield, the CEO of the mid-market consultancy BearingPoint, told Business Insider. AI has disrupted the industry much more rapidly, significantly increasing the level of tech involvement in almost every project, he said.
"Very rarely do we do a project that doesn't have some technology element to it," said Farnfield.
Many firms are now moving toward an "Accenture model" that integrates business strategy with technology and execution in a combined offering.
One of the key drivers leading that transformation is economics. Over the last five years, technology-related services have outperformed the broader market, growing two to six times as fast as traditional sectors, said Czerniawska, the CEO of Source Global. The demand has led "every firm that can do so to invest in their technology services," she said.
"While everyone is offering more technology services, some want to go even further to say, 'If that's what the future looks like, then we need to turn ourselves into a tech services player that just happens to specialize," said Czerniawska.
While the race to become AI native is undeniably on, the industry's reinvention may be more pronounced in pitch than in practice.
In terms of pure tech usage, consulting firms are still "a long way from the frontier of what's possible" with AI, Charlie Cheesman, a former senior AI consultant at EY, who helped to write the firm's UK AI strategy, told Business Insider.
Professional services firms' strength lies in "initiating large-scale organizational change," he said.
They "were never built to be technical organizations," he said, so they are having to change massively to keep up with AI progress.
Not every firm is rushing to recast itself as a technology company.
"I don't know if the identity of our firm is changing as a result of this," Errol Gardner, global head of consulting at EY, told Business Insider. Technology now drives about half of EY's business, and the firm is hiring deeply technical talent, but that doesn't change EY's core proposition.
"What we do is move clients from state A to state B in a safer way and as value-enabled a way as possible," said Gardner, and AI is a "new tool in the toolbox" to help with that.
Deploying AI at an enterprise-wide scale requires the kind of work consulting firms have long done — navigating regulation, data governance, organizational resistance, and budgets. "They need a business strategy that is powered by AI as opposed to a separate AI strategy," said Gardner.
The identity of a consulting job — being client-facing, delivering value to clients, developing the teams, and working collaboratively — hasn't fundamentally changed, he said.
PwC's Wood struck a similar note: "It's tempting to look at AI and think the firm needs to become a technology company," he said, but PwC's approach is to focus on how to become the best version of itself using AI.
"The real shift in consulting is not from strategy to implementation, or from generalists to specialists. It is that enterprise problems are now more interconnected," Kate Smaje, global leader of technology and AI at McKinsey, told Business Insider.
The employee experience
Five employees from top consulting firms — Deloitte, KPMG, and McKinsey — all said the job was undoubtedly more tech-heavy, but that AI's impact on consulting jobs is more complex than simply turning them into technologists.
Every employee at McKinsey has become more technical than they were three years ago, said Louis-Charles Généreux, an associate partner at McKinsey, who first joined the firm in 2018. Using AI to enhance work has become a crucial part of remaining competitive in the industry, he said.
At Deloitte, AI hasn't caused the work to change overnight, said a US-based technology consultant who has been at the firm for six years. Instead, it's slowly shifted the job from creation to validation and has increased expectations for workers. "Teams are now expected to deliver more with the same or fewer people," the consultant said.
A senior consultant at Deloitte UK said that even after clients implement AI tools, they still return to the firm needing ongoing support. The "core identity of the profession remains rooted in adaptability," the consultant said.
Others said that, while leadership narratives emphasize AI in everything they do, daily use still mostly leans on generative AI rather than agentic AI.
Cheesman, the former EY AI consultant, said the industry's ability to deploy AI has yet to match the technology's potential: Consultancies can move clients "one or two steps forward" when AI could be taking them 5 or 10 steps forward.
There is no shortage of highly intelligent, capable people in the industry, Cheesman said, but 99% are not coders.
For now, it's still unclear how far consulting firms will go toward remaking themselves as technology companies. They may offer more technology services than they did a decade ago, but most clients still think of the top strategy firms as doing strategy, and the Big Four predominantly as doing finance-related work, said Source Global's Czerniawska. Ultimately, she added, it's for clients to decide the firm's identity, not vice versa.
Around 90% of clients believe AI will affect how firms deliver their services, yet the share who expect that impact to be significant has fallen — from 60% in 2024 to 40% more recently, according to Source Global's research.
There are also advantages to maintaining the consulting identity. Firms that lean too much towards presenting themselves as technology companies face a pricing risk, said Czerniawska. Clients associate technology with lower costs than traditional consulting, she said. Move too far in that direction, and firms risk eroding the premium they charge.
"Identities have shifted unquestionably, but they've not moved to a point where somebody's saying, 'this is a technology company,'" said Czerniawska.
results.summary:
Major consulting firms are rapidly integrating artificial intelligence into their service models, forcing a strategic shift that increasingly blurs the traditional lines between professional advisory and technology companies.

### Key Points
- Firms like KPMG, PwC, and McKinsey are embedding AI across their operations, with some reporting that tech-focused services now account for over 40% of global revenue.
- Major consultancies are aggressively hiring thousands of data and AI professionals while introducing new technical career tracks to meet client demand for implementation.
- Partnerships with AI leaders including OpenAI, Nvidia, and Microsoft are enabling firms to automate junior-level tasks and offer clients direct access to AI-enhanced platforms.
- Despite the "AI-native" branding, industry experts note that most firms remain focused on organizational change rather than becoming pure-play technology developers.
- Research from Source Global indicates that while clients expect AI to impact service delivery, many remain skeptical about the extent of this transformation.

### Why it Matters
The shift toward AI-driven services allows consulting firms to capture higher-growth revenue streams while remaining essential intermediaries for Fortune 500 companies navigating digital transformation. However, firms must carefully balance their new technical identities with their traditional premium pricing models to avoid being commoditized as low-cost software providers.

results.title: Is this the end of the GTA 6 leaks? Take-Two's legal crusade appears to shut down the hubs behind them
results.author: Vikki Blake
results.content:
UPDATE 3.30pm: Despite the CyberLeek website going dark, nope, the GTA 6 leaks haven't stopped.
A seventh clip has reportedly surfaced online, with gameplay details being discussed on Reddit, suggesting whoever is behind the leaks still has access to unreleased footage even with one of their main hubs offline.
Original story follows.
ORIGINAL STORY 12.30pm BST: Take-Two's legal offensive against the source of the ongoing GTA 6 leaks appears to have claimed its first scalp: the CyberLeek website, one of the group's main hubs, has gone offline.
The group's Telegram channel has also gone dark, now displaying only the message "This channel is unavailable due to copyright infringement".
The disappearance comes just days after Take-Two filed subpoenas targeting Microsoft and Discord, seeking information that could identify whoever is behind the CyberLeek persona. Both companies have until 4th September to hand over relevant account data.
The leaks – which have been popping up all week – have been substantive, showing co-protagonist Jason tearing around Vice City in a supercar and shooting the word "leek" into a wall, suggesting some kind of playable access to GTA 6.
As Bertie summarised for us at the time, CyberLeek has maintained that it's doing the leaks in the name of gamers' rights, but behind it is a shady cryptocurrency scheme involving a $CYBERLEEK meme coin the group wants people to buy (and thereby increase the value of) to vote for new video leaks. Ostensibly, this is being done to fund "a secret project", but as Polygon reported, there's evidence to suggest dodgy-seeming personal gain.
There's been a lot of confusion around the Telegram channel, with some Redditors insisting CyberLeek never operated one in the first place and that any Telegram activity attributed to the account was the work of impersonators reposting genuine leaks.
Others maintain the Telegram and website were the only channels CyberLeek confirmed as legitimate. Either way, whichever of those hubs actually belonged to CyberLeek has been nuked along with the website.
It's not clear whether the takedown is directly linked to Take-Two's subpoenas or a separate copyright enforcement action, and Eurogamer has asked Rockstar for comment.
Whether this actually marks the end of the leaks, or just a pause while whoever's behind them regroups elsewhere, remains to be seen.
Take-Two Boss Strauss Zelnick has said he isn't concerned that the company's legal battle could impact Grand Theft Auto 6 sales. The game was made available to pre-order late last month, and immediately became a top seller on the PlayStation Store around the world.
GTA 6 is still slated to release on 19th November 2026, launching on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S.
results.summary:
Take-Two Interactive has successfully forced the CyberLeek website and associated Telegram channel offline as part of an ongoing legal effort to stop unauthorized leaks of Grand Theft Auto 6.

### Key Points
- Take-Two Interactive filed subpoenas against Microsoft and Discord to identify the individuals behind the CyberLeek persona.
- Despite the removal of primary leak hubs, a seventh clip of unreleased GTA 6 gameplay has reportedly surfaced on Reddit.
- The CyberLeek group allegedly used the leaks to promote a cryptocurrency scheme involving a $CYBERLEEK meme coin.
- Grand Theft Auto 6 remains scheduled for a November 19, 2026, release on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S.

### Why it Matters
These leaks highlight the significant security challenges major publishers face when protecting highly anticipated intellectual property from bad actors. While Take-Two maintains that the incident will not impact long-term sales, the situation underscores the growing intersection between gaming leaks and illicit financial schemes.

results.title: AI’s Absurd Spending Boom? Hyperscalers Are Spending 102% of Cloud Revenue on Capex
results.author: Rich Duprey
results.content:
The artificial intelligence boom is turning corporate capital spending into a different kind of arms race. The biggest cloud companies aren’t merely adding data centers as demand grows; they’re building infrastructure years ahead of expected usage.
UBS now estimates hyperscaler capital expenditures could reach about $4.1 trillion from 2026 through 2028. That’s more than three times the $1.292 trillion spent across the previous six years, based on UBS’s hyperscaler spending estimates. For investors, the message is clear: AI is pushing the industry’s long-term spending base into territory that would have looked absurd just a few years ago.
Cloud Revenue Tells The Story
UBS estimates Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN | AMZN Price Prediction), Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG), and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) will collectively spend about 102% of their cloud revenue on capital expenditures in 2026.
That doesn’t mean these companies are burning through more cash than they generate. Their businesses are much larger and more diversified than cloud infrastructure alone. Instead, the ratio shows how aggressively cloud revenue is being recycled into AI infrastructure.
UBS expects that ratio to ease to roughly 99% of cloud revenue in 2027 and 94% in 2028. Yet spending keeps rising.
UBS projects total hyperscaler capex at $492 billion in 2025, $1.009 trillion in 2026, $1.447 trillion in 2027, and $1.619 trillion in 2028 — three times more in three years than in the previous six years combined. It shows how the growth rate can slow while the dollar amount continues climbing.
And the composition matters, too. Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, and Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) account for the largest portions of the buildout, but SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) is making up for lost time, and Oracle (NYSE:ORCL), neocloud providers, and newer entrants are expanding the spending pool.
That means the AI infrastructure opportunity is spreading beyond the handful of companies investors typically associate with the boom.
$4.1 Trillion Is A Bigger Bet Than It Looks
The cumulative UBS estimates for 2026 through 2028 are staggering:
| Company | 2026-2028 Capex | 
| Alphabet | ~$938 billion | 
| Meta Platforms | ~$683 billion | 
| Microsoft | ~$672 billion | 
| Amazon | ~$628 billion | 
| SpaceX | ~$335 billion | 
| Oracle | ~$276 billion | 
| CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV) | ~$130 billion | 
| Nebius Group (NASDAQ:NBIS) | ~$93 billion | 
Together, those figures illustrate why this isn’t simply another upgrade cycle for servers. New demand is coming from traditional hyperscalers, neocloud providers, and SpaceX, creating additional pools of infrastructure spending.
For chipmakers, networking companies, data-center power suppliers, and infrastructure operators, the spending becomes revenue somewhere in the supply chain.
More importantly, the UBS forecast suggests the spending isn’t peaking when the growth rate peaks. Total hyperscaler capex rises from $1.009 trillion in 2026 to $1.619 trillion in 2028. In other words, the industry could be spending more than $1.6 trillion annually even after the initial acceleration begins to moderate.
That’s what makes this different from a normal technology upgrade. AI could reset the industry’s capital requirements at a permanently higher level.
The Risk Is Spending Without Returns
Granted, $1.619 trillion of annual hyperscaler capex by 2028 creates a formidable hurdle. Companies eventually need AI revenue and cash flow to justify those investments.
That’s where investors should remain selective. A data center doesn’t generate attractive returns merely because it contains expensive GPUs. Capacity has to stay utilized, customers have to pay for it, and AI services have to produce enough revenue to cover depreciation, electricity, financing, and operating costs.
There is also a timing risk. Companies can spend billions today on infrastructure that may take years to reach full utilization. If AI demand grows more slowly than expected, depreciation expenses could rise faster than revenue, pressuring margins and free cash flow.
That said, the scale of the commitment from multiple customers reduces the risk that this is simply one company’s speculative bet. Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta, SpaceX, Oracle, and the neoclouds are collectively building an ecosystem around AI compute.
In short, the spending itself isn’t the investment thesis. The investment thesis is that AI demand becomes large enough to keep this infrastructure productive for years.
UBS’s numbers suggest the major cloud platforms are betting heavily that it will. Smart investors don’t have to match their conviction blindly. They should follow the money — and favor companies positioned to monetize the buildout rather than simply finance it.
Key Takeaway
The 102% figure is less a warning about reckless spending than a measure of how radically AI is changing the cloud economy. With UBS projecting roughly $4.1 trillion of hyperscaler capex from 2026 through 2028, investors should expect AI infrastructure spending to remain a dominant market theme well beyond the current boom.
The opportunity is strongest where spending translates into recurring revenue, high utilization, and durable free cash flow. In the end, the winners won’t necessarily be the companies spending the most. They’ll be the ones turning that unprecedented spending into the highest returns on capital.

results.title: If you bought a Pixel 11 Pro, you should activate this free perk immediately
results.author: Nicholas Sutrich
results.content:
The Google Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL are two very full-featured smartphones. If you're a new Pixel user, you're going to spend days sifting through all the available options and features to find your favorites, but before you begin that long (but fun!) journey, you should focus on securing the freebies that come with every Pixel 11 phone.
I'm specifically talking about the 6-month Gemini Pro subscription that comes for free with your Pixel 11. In the past, I was always prompted to activate this trial during the first-time setup when I got a new Pixel, but this year was different. I had to hunt for the offer to make sure it still existed and, thankfully, it does!
With the Pixel 9 and 10 series, Google offered a full year of Gemini Advanced (now known as Google AI Pro), but the Pixel 11 series lowered that to 6 months. Still, it's hard to argue with 6 free months of Google's AI Pro service, which is roughly a $120 value you get just for owning a Pixel 11.
What is Google AI Pro?
Google renamed Gemini Advanced to Google AI Pro in 2025, and with it came a slew of new tools and benefits compared to the free Gemini model and the Google AI Plus subscription. Here's everything Google AI Pro gets you in 2026:
- 4x higher usage limits in the Gemini app
- 1,000 Google Flow credits (Google's creative studio)
- Gemini 3 Pro in Google Search
- Access to the Jules coding agent with higher limits
- Google Antigravity (Google's agentic development platform)
- 5x higher limits on Gemini Notebook (formerly NotebookLM)
- Gemini in Gmail, Docs, and more
- Google Home Premium (30 days of event history for your Nest devices)
- Gemini in Chrome
- YouTube Premium Lite
- 5TB of cloud storage
There's a lot included with Google AI Pro, but I find only a few things particularly useful. Google Home Premium and YouTube Premium Lite are easily my favorite two features. Subscribing to those features by themselves would normally run you $18 a month, so you can already see how good of a value the Google AI Pro subscription is at the normal $19.99 a month rate.
I don't use the vast majority of the advanced Gemini features here, like Jules, Flow, Antigravity, or Notebook, but those would all be incredible values for anyone who might want to take advantage of everything Gemini offers.
How to activate your free Google AI Pro subscription
Now that you understand why Google AI Pro is worthwhile (and why a free 6-month trial is such a great deal), here's what you need to do to activate the trial:
Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android
1. Open the Gemini app. You can find it in your app drawer.
2. Click the menu button in the top-left corner, then tap the settings gear at the bottom next to your account name.
3. Tap the Start trial button underneath the "Manage subscription" button.
4. Make sure the screen says "With your Pixel 11, you get 6 months for $0," then tap the blue Start trial button.
Beginning a Google AI Pro trial starts a subscription through Google Play, so the next screen will ask you to select a payment method for when the trial ends. Don't worry, you're not going to pay anything right now; Google just wants to set up the subscription so that it cycles through the credits you get with your Pixel 11.
Remember, you can always cancel the subscription before the trial ends if you don't want to pay anything by the listed payment start date.
1. Verify that "6-month free trial" is listed under the "Starting today" section on the subscription screen.
2. Note the starting date for payments. I recommend asking Gemini to set a reminder for this date so you can cancel the subscription if you'd like.
3. Select the payment method you want to use when the trial ends, then hit Subscribe.
4. Congrats! Now you have Google AI Pro for the next 6 months for free!
Now, when you open the Gemini app, you can select from more advanced Gemini models (plus, use Gemini a lot more before you hit the daily limit), use new Gemini tools in Google apps like Gmail and Google Drive, watch YouTube videos ad-free, see 30 days of smart home history (and make advanced queries in the Google Home app), and lots more. Have fun!

One person has received medical treatment after a passenger's laptop caught fire on an American Airlines flight.
The pilot had reported a "cabin fire in the back of the airplane" to air traffic control, saying "the flight attendants are trying to put it out now", according to audio obtained by the BBC's US reporting partner CBS News.
"I think we have about four to five passengers that were burned by the laptop. The laptop is contained about mid-aircraft."
One passenger received medical attention on site and was released after American Airlines Flight 2398 - coming from Atlanta, Georgia - landed at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport in Texas on Friday.
The airline told the BBC that the flight landed safely "after reports of smoke from a customer's device during landing. We thank our crew for their professionalism and swift response to quickly contain the device."
After landing, the aircraft taxied to the gate, and emergency personnel met the aircraft upon arrival, per procedure.
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) warns that lithium batteries, including laptop batteries, are capable of overheating, external "as a result of various factors, including if the battery is damaged, overheated, exposed to water, overcharged, or improperly packed".
The FAA recorded , external58 verified lithium battery air incidents so far this year involving smoke, fire or extreme heat. In the last 20 years, the highest number of incidents was related to battery packs, with 84 cases related to laptops.
Lithium batteries must be stowed in carry-on baggage only, the US regulator says.
In May, a UK-bound EasyJet flight from Egypt was diverted to Rome after a power bank was found to be charging in a passenger's luggage in the hold of the aircraft. The flight was rescheduled for the next day.
The UK's aviation regulator the Civil Aviation Authority has said power banks are causing a growing number of serious issues on flights worldwide, and urged more awareness as portable chargers carry "serious risks" of overheating or catching fire.

results.title: As Flock battles public scrutiny, other police surveillance companies see an opening
results.author: Jaclyn Diaz
results.content:
As Flock battles public scrutiny, other police surveillance companies see an opening
Dozens of people crammed into a conference room for a gathering at a public library in Washington, D.C.
The topic? Automated license plate readers, such as the ones sold by Flock Safety, a company facing major backlash from residents in communities across the country who find themselves deeply unsettled by privacy concerns.
On Monday, members of DeFlock DC, a grassroots group dedicated to ending all contracts between the Metropolitan Police Department and Flock, explained to the group how these controversial cameras work and where they are located throughout the city.
But as Loreal Hawk, a member of DeFlock DC, told the group gathered, automated license plate readers are neither new nor unique to Flock. Competitors such as Axon, Motorola Solutions and Verkada, offer similar products to law enforcement agencies, and have for years.
"We need to cancel these contracts," Hawk said.
Flock has been the target of much of the public's ire, but its rivals have largely avoided it. Now, some of those competitors are trying to cash in on Flock's fall from grace.
More than 130,000 automated license-plate readers, or ALPR's, can be found in cities and towns across the country, according to the crowdsourced database DeFlock.org. The cameras take images of the backs of cars. Law enforcement has increasingly turned to this tool to help solve crime.
"The Flock ALPR technology has captured the public's attention" and spurred a realization that "maybe we don't want to be surveilled all the time," said Andrew Ferguson, a law professor at George Washington University.
But now, he said, Flock is the one that has "the target put on its back."
Why is Flock facing so much heat?
Flock CEO Garrett Langley regularly posts on social media extolling the benefits of his company's tech, often noting that communities are safer because of it. Flock was credited with helping to track the suspect in last year's Brown University shooting, which killed two students and injured nine other people.
"On a very personal level, I go to bed every night very proud of the impact we have in the world," Langley told NPR.
Many automated license plate readers, including Flock's, use AI to capture information such as a vehicle's make, model and color. Police can search Flock's shared national database of these images — including vehicles outside of their own jurisdiction.
That national database is a core point of contention for Flock opponents.
"People got really mad at Flock because they realized that it was a window into a whole network of surveillance," said Matthew Guariglia, a senior policy analyst at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, a digital privacy advocacy group. He strongly opposes the technology broadly, not just Flock's version of it.
With this network "suddenly your cameras are being used to enforce things that you don't agree with or that are not illegal in your town," he said.
In Texas, for instance, deputies used Flock data to help investigate a woman suspected of traveling to have an abortion.
Hits against Flock keep coming. Police officers have been found to use this technology to stalk women. And while Flock allows customers to control the information they share on its network, there are some cases where information was unknowingly shared more widely, including with federal immigration agencies.
In response, the company last week announced a host of changes, including reducing its data retention period and emphasizing safeguards around local data searches.
The ACLU said the changes were largely unsatisfying.
Competitors step in
License plate readers are only one piece of a growing police surveillance industry.
Many law enforcement agencies use integrated tools such as facial recognition, gunshot detectors, predictive policing, drones and real-time crime centers that pull all this information into one central hub used by investigators.
Ferguson, who is also the author of Your Data Will Be Used Against You: Policing in the Age of Self-Surveillance, says in his view, those integrated systems raise far more red flags for privacy than license plate readers alone. Yet, they've drawn almost no large-scale public protest.
Guariglia believes Flock is at the center of the license plate reader firestorm, in part, because of its cameras' visibility.
"Once you know what they look like, you become aware of how ubiquitous they are," he said.
Dozens of communities have turned against Flock amid widespread public backlash. About 100 cities have deactivated cameras, rejected deals or cancelled contracts, according to DeFlock's database. Some, such as Denver and Longmont, Colo., signed contracts with Flock competitors this year, including Axon, a trend reported by 404 Media.
Axon, a multibillion dollar company that provides tech and weapons to law enforcement and the military, says it's positioned to step in amid the "deFlock movement." During Axon's most recent earnings call, CEO Rick Smith told investors that law enforcement agencies are making the switch.
"We're seeing a significant number of agencies want to come over to Axon and convert from existing license plate readers to us." He credited the company's "controls and privacy work."
Axon declined to say how much business the company has gained from cancelled Flock contracts.
When asked how Flock is responding to other providers swooping in on their departing business, Langley said he is unconcerned.
"We will have added seven times the number of new customers that have left us this year," he said.
Langley said he was especially surprised about Denver's move to sign a one-year deal with Axon, after residents voiced concerns over data sharing for immigration enforcement.
"I guess in some ways I scratch my head because that company works with ICE," he said. "They lack the accountability and transparency we have, and so I don't know why they made that choice."
Axon holds several multimillion dollar contracts with the Department of Homeland Security for its products, including body cameras and Tasers.
"For more than 30 years, we've built products to protect life," Axon spokesperson Kate MacKinnon said in an email to NPR. "As new technologies emerge, we know that our customers require solutions that protect data and privacy."
But privacy experts warn the switch to other police surveillance technologies isn't a fix.
"You're just replacing one color of camera for another," Guariglia said. "Those dangers you were concerned about are still going to be there."
results.summary:
Flock Safety faces significant public backlash and contract cancellations over privacy concerns, prompting competitors like Axon and Motorola Solutions to aggressively pursue its law enforcement surveillance market share.

### Key Points
- Grassroots groups like DeFlock DC are actively campaigning to terminate municipal contracts with Flock Safety due to concerns over national data sharing.
- Approximately 100 cities have reportedly deactivated cameras or rejected Flock contracts, with some municipalities switching to competitors like Axon.
- Flock Safety’s national database allows police to track vehicles across jurisdictions, a feature critics argue facilitates overreach and potential misuse.
- Axon CEO Rick Smith confirmed that law enforcement agencies are increasingly transitioning to their platform, citing superior privacy controls.
- Privacy advocates warn that replacing Flock with other surveillance providers does not resolve fundamental issues regarding mass data collection and civil liberties.

### Why it Matters
The shift in market share highlights a growing tension between public demand for privacy and the widespread adoption of automated surveillance technology by law enforcement. While Flock currently bears the brunt of public scrutiny, the industry-wide reliance on integrated data systems suggests that privacy concerns will persist regardless of which specific vendor provides the hardware.

results.title: A 60-year-old geothermal company just became an AI infrastructure play
results.author: Alina Maria Stan
results.content:
Ormat, a geothermal company founded six decades ago, has signed a power purchase agreement with Google for up to 150MW in Nevada and is running enhanced geothermal pilots with Sage Geosystems and SLB. Europe has the same demand problem and is meeting it with restraint rather than contracts.
A company that has been drilling for heat since the 1960s is now an artificial intelligence story. Ormat has agreed to supply Google with up to 150 megawatts of new geothermal capacity in Nevada, through the state utility and a tariff that lets the buyer pay a premium for emerging technology.
Until this year it had never sold directly to large power users at all. Its first data centre agreement, signed in January with Switch, covers about 13 megawatts over 20 years at a plant in western Nevada.
The Google contract is more than ten times that. The projects behind it are expected to come online between 2028 and 2030, with Nevada regulators due to approve the arrangement in the second half of this year.
What data centres are buying is continuity. Geothermal runs day and night regardless of weather, which is the quality that makes it worth more to a computing site than cheaper intermittent power.
Ormat operates about 1.85 gigawatts worldwide and is targeting 2.8 by 2028, using conventional plants and storage alone. It has historically added around 100 megawatts a year.
The bigger bet is enhanced geothermal, which borrows drilling and fracturing techniques from oil and gas to reach hotter rock. Ormat is running pilots with Sage Geosystems and the oil services group SLB, both expected online in late 2027, with individual projects potentially reaching 500 megawatts.
This is not a speculative balance sheet. Revenue reached $662.7mn in the first half of 2026, up 43%, with net profit of $71.2mn, and chief executive Doron Blachar says “all the stars are aligned exactly on time.”
The comparison that flatters him is Fervo Energy. The enhanced geothermal specialist listed in May at a $10bn valuation and is now worth about half that.
Europe has the same demand and a different answer. Denmark has paused grid connections because data centres are overwhelming the cleanest grid on the continent, and the EU has asked households to shift electricity use away from peak hours.
The resource is not the obstacle. Iceland runs on it, Italy has generated geothermal power since 1911, and the deep rock under Germany and the Netherlands is the subject of serious national programmes.
What Nevada has is a contract. Europe wants geothermal to replace natural gas, and while it works out how, the hyperscalers are signing 15-year agreements somewhere else.

results.summary:
Geothermal energy provider Ormat has secured a major power purchase agreement to supply Google with up to 150 megawatts of carbon-free electricity from new Nevada-based projects by 2030.

### Key Points
- Ormat will provide Google with 150 megawatts of geothermal power, with Nevada regulatory approval expected in late 2024.
- The company is expanding its global capacity from 1.85 gigawatts to a target of 2.8 gigawatts by 2028.
- Enhanced geothermal pilots are currently underway in partnership with Sage Geosystems and SLB, with expected completion in 2027.
- Ormat reported $662.7 million in revenue for the first half of 2026, representing a 43% increase over the previous period.
- Unlike intermittent solar or wind, geothermal provides continuous, reliable power essential for the 24/7 operational demands of large-scale data centers.

### Why it Matters
This agreement highlights the growing trend of major technology firms securing long-term, reliable energy sources to support the massive power requirements of artificial intelligence infrastructure. By prioritizing geothermal energy, companies like Google are establishing a blueprint for grid stability that contrasts with the regulatory and supply constraints currently hindering similar projects in Europe.

results.title: I’m quitting Kindle, and Amazon’s new DRM update proves why you should too
results.author: Dhruv Bhutani
results.content:
I'm quitting Kindle, and Amazon's new DRM update proves why you should too
Aug 22, 2026 — 5:00 AM ET
The Kindle Oasis was released in 2019, and it’s been a while since Amazon added a meaningful update to the system. So, when I learned that Amazon was rolling out a new system software update this past week, I was quite excited. That’s until I learned that the update closes a long-standing loophole for library books borrowed via Libby that lets you hold onto a book longer than you’d otherwise be allowed. Additionally, it further tightens DRM to ensure buyers can’t offload books from the Kindle.
While the first feature doesn’t affect me much, the latter, as someone who likes preserving digital media, makes the update an instant no-go for me. On paper, these changes protect publishers’ rights and intellectual property. For the end user, though, they are just another reminder that you never truly own your digital library or even the hardware you technically bought.
Look, I can understand Amazon wanting to safeguard publishers’ contracts, but the company has spent years ignoring basic software features that readers have been begging for while actively stripping away the few workarounds that made the ecosystem bearable. However, this latest move is the final straw for me. I am done trying to stay ahead of Amazon’s shenanigans, and I’m convinced I’m never buying another Kindle. Here’s why.
Would Amazon's DRM restrictions convince you to leave the Kindle ecosystem?
The illusion of digital ownership
Let’s start with the elephant in the room. For years, Kindle users have relied on a clever workaround to manage their reading for borrowed library books. By downloading a book through Libby and immediately putting the device into airplane mode, readers could hold onto their digital loans past the official due date.
Libby loans tend to range from 7 to 21 days. That might sound like a reasonable duration for the average book, but if you read large tomes like “The Wheel of Time,” you know it’s not nearly enough. You might be a slow reader, or you might just be busy with work and life, but the trick bought you extra time to read.
When a corporation can change how your e-reader works after you buy it, how much of the experience do you truly own?
The thing is, on Libby’s end, the book was still returned to the library system on time for the next person in line, but the local file remained readable on the disconnected device. Amazon has now closed this gap entirely by implementing an on-device digital timer. When your loan expires, the book locks up regardless of whether you are connected to the internet.
I understand why Amazon and publishers wanted to shut this down. Digital library licenses are expensive and complicated, and authors deserve proper compensation for their work.
But taking this option away stings because it highlights a much bigger problem with modern e-readers. You are increasingly renting access not just to your content, but also to your hardware. Every time Amazon pushes a silent background update, it proves that the device in your hands is really just a remote storefront disguised as hardware, and the company can change or even remove functionality you’re accustomed to.
When a corporation can change how your e-reader works after you buy it to protect its bottom line, without any heads-up, how much of the experience do you truly own?
The fences keep getting higher
The crackdown does not stop with library loans. Amazon has also tightened its digital rights management protocols, targeting how files are handled on older hardware like my Kindle Oasis. This makes it much harder to back up your purchased books or manage collections through third-party software like Calibre.
Amazon clearly wants users to only buy books through the Kindle storefront, and it is willing to put up massive digital walls to keep users from looking elsewhere. The idea is pretty simple: once you’ve built up a sizable ebook library that can’t be read anywhere but on a Kindle, there’s less incentive for you to look at alternative ebook readers, no matter how much better the hardware experience is.
Previously, I could buy a book from the Kindle storefront, strip out the DRM and keep a clean copy for my personal library and archival purposes. That’s no longer an option.
Amazon can delete, update, or even remove access to a book at will.
As someone deep into the Kindle ecosystem, I can confirm that enthusiasts are exhausted from playing this game. When you buy a physical paperback, you can lend it to a friend, sell it to a used bookstore, or let it sit on your shelf. Digital books don’t have those advantages. In fact, there have been instances where Amazon retroactively made changes to a published book. I care about things like editions. I care about things like reading the first version of a book ever published because it represents the author’s raw thoughts rather than whatever edits the publisher made.
The fact that I can no longer retain a copy of that version rubs me the wrong way. By locking down ebooks through multiple layers of encryption, Amazon leaves me with no control over the book at all. Amazon can delete, update, or even remove access to a book at will.
Users who have spent thousands of dollars building a digital library are realizing that they could lose access to their favorite books whenever Amazon decides to change its software policies, and it does that often enough.
New hardware, same old limitations
For a brand that is as slow-moving as it is, it’s not all been terrible. Amazon has finally made some moves on the hardware front. We finally got a color e-ink display with the Kindle Colorsoft, addressing a years-long request from comic book fans and readers who wanted vibrant cover art. But you only have to look at Kobo and Boox to see just how far ahead of Kindle their ecosystems are.
Hardware updates are nice, but Amazon continues to neglect the actual software experience. The operating system on a modern Kindle feels almost identical to what we were using a decade ago, minus the useful features Amazon has stripped away over time. A quick look at the Kindle community online reveals a massive list of basic software features that Amazon simply refuses to build.
Hardware updates are nice, but Amazon continues to neglect the actual software experience.
Users have been begging for native Bluetooth support for page-turners, allowing people to turn pages wirelessly without clipping bulky third-party clamps onto the screen bezel. Readers want proper directory organization — things like real nested subfolders inside collections so you can sort an author’s work by series instead of dumping hundreds of titles into one flat list.
We still cannot set custom lock-screen wallpapers without tedious jailbreaks, and basic reading statistics, such as daily page counts or a persistent progress bar, remain completely absent. Amazon has the engineering resources to build complex anti-piracy lockouts, yet it cannot provide users with simple operating system controls that budget competitors included years ago.
Kindle Unlimited is not the answer
Amazon’s locking down the DRM and Libby loopholes makes sense when you see what the company wants you to do. The company would love for you to sign up for Kindle Unlimited instead. The company pushes its monthly subscription service across lock screens, homepages, and navigation menus. The pitch sounds great on the surface because you pay a fixed monthly fee for unlimited reading. Leaving aside the fact that people in general, and readers in particular, are absolutely tired of being pushed subscriptions, the reality of the catalog is far less impressive.
Kindle Unlimited cannot replace a public library. Not until it gets rid of the slop problem. 
If you spend time browsing Kindle Unlimited, you will find a massive collection of self-published titles, serialized novellas, and niche releases, but very few mainstream bestsellers or new releases from major publishers. I’m not going to say that self-publishing is bad — there is certainly good content in the mix — but there’s more slop than substance in the mix, and it certainly cannot replace a public library. Amazon expects users to pay a recurring fee for a restricted catalog while simultaneously shutting down the methods people used to read actual library bestsellers on their own terms.
It is an aggressive business strategy that alienates the exact audience of readers who helped build the Kindle brand in the first place.
The competition is just doing it better
This latest update is the breaking point for my loyalty to Amazon. People are already leaving the Kindle ecosystem, and anti-consumer moves like these will only accelerate the shift. We are no longer living in an era where Amazon has a monopoly on quality e-readers. The competition has caught up, and in many ways, rival platforms have blown past Amazon in software flexibility and user freedom.
Brands like Kobo offer devices with integrated OverDrive support, seamless Instapaper integration for web articles, and native support for open file formats like EPUB without requiring cloud conversions or going through Amazon’s servers.
We are no longer living in an era where Amazon has a monopoly on quality e-readers.
Meanwhile, Android-based e-ink tablets from brands like Boox let you install any reading app you choose, giving you much more freedom over where you buy your books. These platforms treat you like an adult who owns a piece of hardware rather than a subscriber trapped inside a walled ecosystem. In fact, Boox isn’t even trying to build an alternate ecosystem.
Combine that with self-hosted apps like BookLore and Calibre, and you have a bona fide Kindle ecosystem replacement that’s entirely under your own control. That’s the route I’ve taken, and it is becoming the go-to choice for most enthusiasts.
It’s time to vote with your wallet
In 2026, the convenience of the Kindle ecosystem is no longer worth the trade-offs it asks you to make. I am tired of waking up to software updates that make my device less capable than it was when I bought it. On my end, I’ve jailbroken my Kindle and used an update blocker to safeguard myself. But the fact is I shouldn’t have to.
The closure of the Libby workaround and the tightening of DRM show exactly where Amazon places its priorities. The company cares about locked-in subscription revenue and publisher deals, not the user experience. That lack of consumer-centricity is precisely why I’ll switch device families when it’s time to upgrade.
As consumers, our only leverage is where we choose to spend our money. My current Kindle will be the last one I ever buy, and it might be time for you to look at Kindle alternatives as well.
results.summary:
Amazon’s latest Kindle software update has sparked backlash by closing a popular Libby library-loan loophole and tightening DRM restrictions, prompting users to reconsider their loyalty to the platform.

### Key Points
- Amazon implemented an on-device digital timer that automatically locks Libby library books once the loan period expires, even in airplane mode.
- New DRM protocols restrict users from managing or backing up purchased ebooks using third-party software like Calibre.
- The update affects older hardware, including the Kindle Oasis, limiting the ability of users to preserve or archive their digital libraries.
- Critics argue Amazon prioritizes subscription services like Kindle Unlimited and publisher contracts over user-requested features like custom wallpapers and better file organization.
- Competitors such as Kobo and Boox are gaining traction by offering more flexible, open-format support and greater control over hardware and software.

### Why it Matters
These changes highlight the growing tension between corporate digital rights management and the consumer expectation of true ownership over purchased media. As Amazon continues to restrict device functionality through silent updates, users are increasingly shifting toward open-ecosystem alternatives that offer more autonomy and long-term control over their digital libraries.

results.title: I switched to the HyperDrive Next Thunderbolt 5 dock for a few weeks, and it could be the best accessory for productivity masters — here's why
results.author: c.cale.hunt@gmail.com (Cale Hunt) , Cale Hunt
results.content:
Windows Central Verdict
The HyperDrive Next Thunderbolt 5 Dock brings a potent combination of a built-in M.2 SSD slot and Thunderbolt Share certification, perfect for busy offices involving multiple PCs. However, its lack of native video output and so-so charging capabilities might have you looking at the competition.
Pros
- +Nice design with aluminum shell
- +Built-in M.2 SSD slot
- +Certified for Thunderbolt Share
- +2.5Gb Ethernet port is handy
- +Triple 4K external display support
Cons
- -Some issues with simultaneous M.2 SSD and 2.5Gb Ethernet usage
- -Only works horizontally
- -No native video ports
- -Plastic faceplates
- -Relatively weak charging from most ports
Why you can trust Windows Central
Docking stations are an interesting section of the laptop market. There are a lot of options out there, many of them offering the latest Thunderbolt 5 connectivity with an assortment of older and varied ports.
As the market fills up, laptop docks have to set themselves apart with different sub-features. I'm talking about Thunderbolt Share. A built-in M.2 SSD slot. A standout design (as much as that's possible with a small chunk of metal).
In the case of Hyper's HyperDrive Next Thunderbolt 5 dock that I've been using for a few weeks, it's the extra features that I'm most excited about. Let me explain so you know if it's right for your desk.
This review was made possible thanks to a review sample provided by HyperDrive. It had no input nor saw the contents of this review prior to publication.
I've been testing docking stations since before the Thunderbolt 3 era, and I have a clear idea of what's good and what isn't. I'm here to give you an unbiased look at HyperDrive's new dock so that you can make the right buying decision.
Where can I buy the HyperDrive Next Thunderbolt 5 dock?
The HyperDrive Next Thunderbolt 5 dock is available at major online retailers, including Amazon and B&H. Although it launched with a $399.99 price tag, it seems like it's now permanently available at $319.99.
For comparison's sake, the CalDigit TS5 Plus — currently my favorite Thunderbolt 5 dock on the market — costs almost $800.
Wavlink's Thunderbolt 5 dock, which I favorably reviewed, costs about $299.99 before frequent discounts (often falling to less than $200), while Kensington's excellent SD7100T5 EQ Pro costs about $339.
I'd say that Hyper's HyperDrive Next dock is priced within reason compared to other Thunderbolt 5 hardware, although Wavlink continues to be the best value option out there that I've tested.
What sort of ports does the HyperLink Drive have?
Dock design doesn't usually vary too much, and the HyperDrive Next plays it fairly safe with a chunky aluminum shell and plastic faceplates. I've mentioned plenty of times in other reviews that I prefer an all-metal design for added durability and less chance of scratching.
I like the ribbed corners on the aluminum shell. They add a bit of texture to an otherwise sleek exterior, and they help dissipate heat.
The dock works horizontally only, with rubber pads on the bottom to prevent it from slipping. Measuring 7.64 inches (19.4cm) wide and 3.07 inches (7.8cm) deep, it's thankfully rather compact.
There appear to be some holes drilled for mounting with a bracket, though a permanent setup like that might not be ideal due to the M.2 SSD slot's location (more on that in a moment).
The front of the dock includes dual USB-A ports at 10Gbps each, a 3.5mm audio combo jack, and a single downstream Thunderbolt 5 port.
What you might think at first glance are SD card readers are merely vents cut out to help the built-in cooling fan. The slots sit below the power button and LED status light.
The back of the dock is where you'll find two more downstream Thunderbolt 5 ports, an upstream Thunderbolt 5 port for connecting your host laptop, two USB-A (10Gbps) ports, a 2.5Gbps Ethernet jack, dual lock slots, and a 20V power hookup.
The upstream host connection supports device charging at up to 140W, which is enough to keep most laptops without a discrete GPU topped up and ready to go.
At this point, you might be asking where the video outputs are located. Well, you're looking at them. The HyperDrive Next relies entirely on Thunderbolt 5 for external monitor support.
If you're using older monitors without USB-C connectivity, you'll need some adapters that switch the USB-C form factor used by Thunderbolt 5 to HDMI or DisplayPort.
The good news is that Thunderbolt 5 is quite capable of handling video, and the dock allows for up to three 4K external displays, each running at a 60Hz refresh rate. If you're targeting a high resolution, it'll go as high as 8K at 144Hz.
It's worth noting that some other Thunderbolt 5 docks support up to three 4K displays each at 144Hz, so there's definitely a bit being left behind due to the other features on board.
I had no problems running one 4K screen and one ultrawide QHD+ screen off the dock, with bandwidth to add more. As mentioned, I've been using this dock on my desk, and I never noticed it get overly hot despite multiple monitors, frequent data transfers, and connected accessories.
HyperDrive Next's additional Thunderbolt 5 features
Aside from the incredible transfer speeds you get from Thunderbolt 5, the extra bandwidth opens up some extra features that I particularly love.
Like the Razer Thunderbolt 5 Dock Chroma I tested last year, the HyperDrive Next dock comes with a built-in M.2 PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSD slot, with a hatch located on the bottom of the dock.
You need a screwdriver to get in, but it's well worth it, with support for full-size 2280 M.2 sticks all the way down to smaller 2230 drives. You should be able to use up to a 16TB drive in here (who can afford that these days?), doubling the capacity of the other docks I've tested.
The other big feature is Intel Thunderbolt Share. It's a tool that allows Thunderbolt 4 and 5 laptops to communicate directly with each other, easing common transfers and making life with multiple laptops that much easier.
The catch is that at least one of the laptops in use needs to have official Intel Thunderbolt Share certification, unless you have a dock connected in between with the official badge. That's where the HyperDrive Next comes in.
You can connect two separate laptops to the dock and control both from one set of peripherals. File transfers are super easy, requiring just a drag and a drop.
What I don't like about the HyperDrive Next Thunderbolt 5 dock
Depending on how you use your dock, the lack of native video outputs might be a con. However, for others, full Thunderbolt and USB connectivity, paired with an M.2 slot and Thunderbolt Share, might be exactly what's needed.
The only major issue I experienced has to do with how the dock handles heavy workloads. While testing, I noticed drops in SSD and Ethernet speeds when used simultaneously.
I figured this had something to do with power allotment. A 180W adapter isn't that big for a dock that can charge a laptop at 140W. Indeed, this does make some of the charging abilities on ports other than the host connection fairly wimpy.
The other Thunderbolt 5 ports only charge at 15W, and one USB-A port hits 7.5W. The rest sit at a rather low 4.5W.
However, after doing a bit of research, it seems that the Ethernet/SSD limitation is caused by the actual Intel Barlow Ridge chipset that's used by modern Thunderbolt 5 docks.
So, yes, the dock is super convenient thanks to its built-in features. But you probably won't get as good of performance as if you had a drive and an Ethernet cable connected separately via Thunderbolt 5 ports. It's not exactly Hyper's fault, but it's well worth noting.
Should you buy the HyperDrive Next Thunderbolt 5 dock?
✅ You should buy this if ...
- You want a Thunderbolt 5 dock with a built-in M.2 SSD slot and Thunderbolt Share.
- You have a Thunderbolt 5 laptop that can take advantage of all features (or you plan on buying one soon and can make do with Thunderbolt 4 speeds for the time being).
❌ You should not buy this if ...
- You want maximum SSD and Ethernet speeds without requiring any adapters.
- You have three external 4K displays and want to run them all at 144Hz.
Hyper's HyperDrive Next Thunderbolt 5 dock is a high-end option that actually competes quite well with the competition in terms of pricing and performance.
For example, the Kensington SD7100T5 EQ Pro comes with a built-in M.2 SSD slot, tons of ports (including SD card readers), and 2.5Gb Ethernet. It does not have Thunderbolt Share. It costs about $340.
If you don't need Thunderbolt Share or a built-in SSD slot, the Wavlink Thunderbolt 5 Thunderlight is probably a better bet, especially at only about $220.
Sitting in between is the HyperDrive Next at about $320, and I'd recommend it to those who want the convenience of external M.2 SSD storage and the ability to quickly share content between two PCs.
Otherwise, I recommend checking out my guide to the best laptop docking stations on the market today for more great options.
The HyperDrive Next Thunderbolt 5 Dock brings a potent combination of a built-in M.2 SSD slot and Thunderbolt Share certification, perfect for busy offices involving multiple PCs. However, its lack of native video output and so-so charging capabilities might have you looking at the competition.

Reuters reports "a major success in a new field of cancer treatment this week, as Moderna and Merck announced a personalized mRNA cancer vaccine "reduced the risk of recurrence and spread of melanoma in a late-stage trial".  The vaccine was tested with Merck's widely used immunotherapy drug Keytruda:
Thousands of patients who have undergone surgery to remove high-risk melanoma tumors could benefit as soon as next year if regulators approve the vaccine, Moderna President Stephen Hoge said in an interview. This is the first positive late-stage trial result for an mRNA cancer vaccine, which trains a patient's immune system to fight tumors by targeting specific mutations in those cells, and the first such study to show that adding a treatment to Keytruda worked better than that therapy alone... Interim results of the ongoing study, released on Wednesday, found the treatment, Intismeran, met both its primary target of reducing cancer recurrence and its secondary goal of preventing tumors from spreading to other parts of the body, compared with Keytruda alone. When the vaccine is injected into a patient, the patient's cells produce copies of mutations for the immune system to recognize and destroy... Merck said the companies are already in talks with regulators about the treatment.
 
"Merck, Moderna and other companies are testing similar approaches against lung, breast and pancreatic cancers," the article points out. It adds that Karen Knudsen, CEO of the Parker Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy, "said the Moderna results could signal a new era for treating solid-tumor cancers."
 
More from CNN: The trial result is "a monumental leap forward," validating mRNA technology as a cancer treatment, said Dr. Julie Gralow, chief medical officer of the American Society of Clinical Oncology...
